newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pilots union warns Air Liberte could go bust.
newsitem.headline: Pilots union warns Air Liberte could go bust.

text.p: The SNPL French pilot's union said on Saturday that airline Air Liberte was laying off staff and cutting back its fleet and risked liquidation as creditors were unsatisfied with a British Airways Plc rescue bid.
"There are serious problems with the creditors. They are not satisfied with the offer made by BA and Banque Rivaud, Air Liberte risks liquidation," Serge Martinez of the SNPL told Reuters.
He said the court-appointed administrators had already twice been given an extension of the period to reach a settlement with creditors and the latest deadline was for January 8.
The commercial court of Creteil decided late October not to liquidate debt-laden Air Liberte after a rescue bid by British Airways and Rivaud, a founding shareholder of the regional airline.
BA would take a 70 percent stake in Air Liberte with the rest owned by Rivaud and the two companies would make a 630 million franc capital injection. BA already owns TAT in France.
The SNPL said that contracts with 600 temporary staff had not been extended while between 108 and 117 staff were being fired, among which 54 pilots or a third of the total.
It added that Air Liberte had returned five Airbus planes to U.S. lease company ILFC and was cutting its fleet of McDonnell Douglas DC-10s to three from five.
The DC-10s will be used for flights to the French Antilles and Martinique while seven MD-83 jets will be used within France in association with TAT.
Last summer, Air Liberte had 2,000 staff of which 1,150 were staff and the rest worked on contracts.

Martinez said creditors such as Tunis Air, which handled Air Liberte ground services in Tunesia, and leasing firm ILFC were not happy with the BA/Rivaud bid of a 20 percent cash payment of debts or an alternative payment over 10 years.
Air Liberte owns some 800 million francs to its creditors.
"There are dissatisfied. They say that Rivaud as an original shareholder is partly responsible for the debts and should pay more," Martinez said.
There was no immediate reaction from British Airways or Rivaud, a private financial holding company.
